learning_outcomes.text: To use basic laws of electromagnetism to solve simple problems in electromagnetism or electromechanics (LO 1.1, LO 1.2).
To use vector formalism to express interaction forces, in vacuum, between a magnetic field and moving particles or a current, or between currents.
To use Biot-Savart and Ampere laws in vacuum to calculate the magnetic field produced by currents travelling in geometrically simple structures.
To calculate the trajectory of a charged particle through a uniform and constant magnetic field.
To distinguish the magnetic properties of various materials (dia-,para-,ferro-magnetic) based on their magnetic permeability.
To explain and interpret the effect on a coil inductance when a ferromagnetic core is introduced.

To explain the hysteresis phenomenon of magnetic materials, and use the magnetic permeability in the derivation of inductances or simple magnetic circuits containing linear or non-linear magnetic materials.
To explain the origin of energy losses in a conducting or ferromagnetic material for AC regime.
To explain and justify the boundary conditions for B and H at the interface between two different media.
To define the inductance and mutual inductance of simple structures with and without a ferromagnetic core.
To explain the Lenz-Faraday law expressing the e.f.m induced by a variable magnetic flux and use it for the calculation of AC generators with geometrically simple structures.
To calculate the magnetic energy stored in simple circuits or structures.
To explain how simple electromechanical systems like a DC motor, a AC generator, an ideal transformer, an electromagnet work by exploiting the notion of magnetic flux.
To write and explain Maxwell equations for the EM field in their integral formulation limited to the static case.
To express in vector form the equations of motion of one or several interconnected rigid bodies.
To derive the equations describing the dynamics of a single rigid body (Newton-Euler equations).
To manipulate generalized coordinates to model multiple rigid bodies dynamics and to derive their equations of motion as well as the constraint forces via the Virtual Power Principle.
To use the tools associated with the geometrical space allowing to manipulate vectors in the 3D space.
To use the systematic procedure to calculate, in a general frame, the successive temporal derivatives of a vector in a mobile base.
To describe in the 3D space, the instantaneous configurations of one or several interconnected rigid bodies.
To specify the variables describing the dynamic behavior of a body modeled as a continuous medium (mass center, momentum, angular momentum, kinetic energy) with an application to the rigid body case.
To use and manipulate the concept of the inertial matrix of a rigid body to mathematically express its angular momentum and kinetic energy.

To exploit various properties (symmetry, planes figures) to easily derive the mass center position as well as the inertial matrix of a geometrically simple body or combination of various geometrically simple bodies.
To express the vector motion equations of a rigid body submitted to various forces (Newton-Euler equations).

For a rigid body first, then for a system of interconnected rigid bodies, to make a justified choice of a set of generalized coordinates allowing an optimized description of the configurations of the system (in 3D /2D space).

For a rigid body first, then for a system of interconnected rigid bodies, to express the constraints ' holonomic and non-holonomic ' involving the generalized coordinates (or velocities), and verify their independence.
To determine the number of degrees of freedom of a mechanical system.
To make the inventory of forces (and torques) influencing the dynamic behavior of such a system.
To write the motion equations for such a system as a function of generalized coordinates and their derivatives.
To make use of the virtual power principle to derive the differential equations describing the behavior of rigid systems, avoiding the calculation of link forces.
To explain the various kinds of links or static supports, and related degrees of freedom and constraints.

syllabus_topics: Dynamics characterization of a rigid body

assessment_methods.method: Written exam on 'rigid body mechanics' part
Optional test on 'electromagnetism' part during the semester

assessment_rules: Students are evaluated individually via a written exam during the session. The 'electromagnetism' part counts for 40% and the 'rigid body mechanics' part for 60% of the final grade, unless one part is graded below 10/20. An optional test on the 'electromagnetism' part is typically organized during the semester and counts for 30% of the grade of the 'electromagnetism' part, if advantageous to the student. Only an unannotated form, provided at the beginning of the year, is allowed for the written examination.
